candidates.statement: In the preamble to the 1993 final rule, the Agency stated that the study sponsor and/or drug 82 manufacturer should not separate out the reserve samples of the T and RS before sending the 83 drug product to the testing site. 9 This is to ensure that the reserve samples are in fact 84 representative of the drug product provided by the study sponsor and/or drug manufacturer for 85 the testing. The study sponsor and/or drug manufacturer should send shipment (s) of the T and 86 RS to the testing site so that the testing site can randomly select samples to retain as reserve 87 samples, and samples for testing. Generally, the drug product should also be maintained in the 88 study sponsor’s and/or drug manufacturer’s original container (see section IV). 89

candidates.statement: This revised guidance 11 clarifies the recommendations related to the handling and retention of 115 reserve samples: 116  Section III clarifies the types of in vivo and in vitro studies for which an applicant or its 117 CRO is required to retain reserve samples. 118  Section IV.A. updates the sampling techniques recommended in the 2004 Guidance to 119 reflect that generally reserve samples should be selected by the testing sites prior to 120 conducting the BA or BE study and provides new recommendations on how to handle 121 reserve samples for co-packaged products, blinded studies, and repackaged products. 122  Section IV.B. describes the conditions under which FDA generally does not intend to 123 enforce the requirement to retain a sufficient quantity to perform five times all the release 124 tests required in the application or supplemental application. This section of the guidance 125 is final and for immediate implementation. 126  Section IV.C. clarifies FDA’s recommendations for each testing site regarding the 127 retention of reserve samples for multiple studies, multiple batches, and multiple 128 shipments. 129  Section IV.D. discusses FDA’s recommendations regarding access to and storage of 130 reserve samples, including the appropriate tracking and documentation of transfers of 131 reserve samples. 132  Section V clarifies the responsibilities of the stakeholders (i.e., study sponsor, drug 133 manufacturer, testing site, investigator, CRO, SMO, etc.) for the handling and retention 134 of reserve samples in various study settings. 135

candidates.statement: The study sponsor and/or drug manufacturer should clarify to the testing sites whether reserve 139 samples are required to be retained under §§320.38 and 320.63. Where a study sponsor and/or 140 drug manufacturer determines that reserve samples are required to be retained, FDA 141 recommends, as a best practice, documenting a detailed plan for the handling and retention of 142 reserve samples in the study protocol and describing the procedures followed and what was 143 retained in the study report. It is recommended that the study protocol and study report include: 144 the method for random selection of the reserve samples; the testing site staff responsible for 145 selecting the reserve samples for retention; the total quantity of reserve samples; the number of 146 shipments of study drug (T and RS) to each testing site; and the number of reserve samples from 147 each shipment. This information will help support evaluation of the study’s integrity. 148

Please note, however, that not 171 all in vitro studies are BE studies, and in vitro studies that are not BE studies are not subject to 172 the regulations for reserve samples. For example, applicants may conduct in vitro 173 characterization studies that compare test and reference products but that are not in vitro BE 174 studies. An in vitro BE study typically should have well-defined statistical equivalence criteria 175 and endpoints. Generally, product-specific guidances (PSGs) explicitly describe in vitro tests as 176 either in vitro BE studies or in vitro characterization studies. FDA recommends that reserve 177 samples be retained for all studies that PSGs describe as in vitro BE studies. FDA inspections have revealed that selecting reserve samples from 196 leftover testing samples (samples not administered to subjects or used in the study) has left 197 some study sites with insufficient quantities to retain as reserve samples, and improper storage 198 of reserve samples not in the original containers or in multiple open containers. As such, 199 leftover samples should not be retained as reserve samples, unless the study involves use of a 200 single container of bulk packaged single-dose unit product as described below. This will help 201 ensure that the reserve samples are in fact representative of the drug product provided by the 202 study sponsor and/or drug manufacturer and used in the BA or BE study, that they are retained 203 in sufficient quantity and in accordance with storage requirements, and that they are retained in 204 the study sponsor’s and/or drug manufacturer’s original container. For example, any of the 209 following random sampling techniques might be used by the testing site for the container size 210 and packaging described (italicized text is particularly relevant). 211

candidates.statement: FDA is aware that many study sponsors and/or drug manufacturers (or their SMOs) now use 249 interactive response technology (IRT) for randomization. During inspections, we have seen 250 instances where the study sponsor and/or drug manufacturer or SMO uses IRT to determine 251 which containers to select as reserve samples or otherwise instructs the testing site to select 252 specific pre-numbered containers as reserve samples. As noted above, reserve samples should 253 not be selected by the study sponsor and/or drug manufacturer or other packaging site prior to 254 reaching the testing sites. SMOs should not select reserve samples or tell testing sites which 255 pre-numbered containers to retain as reserve samples (even when the selection is based on the 256 use of IRT), because SMOs involved in packaging the T and RS (and P, as applicable) would 257 know the identity of the individually numbered containers, and therefore such pre-selection 258 could compromise the integrity of the study. This disrupts random selection and sometimes 259 breaks the blinding of samples absent a clinical safety issue necessitating the unblinding. Study 260 sponsors and/or drug manufacturers, SMOs, or other individuals should not instruct testing sites 261 to select a specific pre-numbered container(s) as reserves; rather, testing sites should randomly 262 select a sufficient quantity of the pre-numbered containers to retain as reserve samples. 263

candidates.statement: To ensure that reserve samples are representative of what was used in the BA or BE study as 372 required by §§ 320.38(a) and 320.63, generally each testing site should randomly select a 373 sufficient quantity as described above in section IV.B. from each shipment for each BA or BE 374 study. We recognize that certain BE studies, such as comparative pharmacodynamic or 375 comparative clinical endpoint BE studies, usually require multiple testing sites and multiple 376 shipments of drug product to testing sites to complete the study. FDA recommends that 377 applicants consider planning or modifying shipping patterns and/or the study design to minimize 378 the number of shipments of drug products to testing sites to the extent possible in order to avoid 379 having to retain excessive quantities of reserve samples. In the rare instance where there may be 380 unusual circumstances that prevent a study from retaining the recommended minimum quantity 381 of reserve samples as described in section IV.B. above, FDA recommends study sponsors and/or 382 drug manufacturers submit their reserve sample plan proposal and justification for the proposal 383 to the Agency for feedback prior to conducting the study. 18
candidates.context: C. Retention for Multiple Shipments, Batches, and Studies 370 For in vivo studies, testing sites do not need to retain reserve samples from every lot or batch, 386 within a single shipment or across multiple shipments, of T and RS used in a BA or BE study. 387 However, FDA recommends as a best practice that study sponsors and/or drug manufacturers 388 should send samples to testing sites in such a manner that the testing sites are able to randomly 389 select reserve samples from the same batch. For example, if there are three different batches of 390 drug product to be used in an in vivo BE study, the study sponsor and/or drug manufacturer 391 could ensure that each shipment to the testing site(s) consists of only one batch of product. This 392 would help ensure that the randomly selected reserve samples by the testing sites are 393 representative of the drug products used in the study.
